lesson.title: Turn messy text into usable columns

lead.text: Put the tally sheet into a pandas Series with one entry per tally: 'Bay', ' bay', 'BAY ' and 'Hill'. Ask pandas how many different shops there are and it answers four. It compares text character by character, so a space counts as a character like any other, and a capital B is a different character from a small b. You read past those differences without noticing, but the computer has no way to.

So the text has to be made consistent before anything is counted or matched. Two small jobs cover most of it. Stripping removes blank characters from both ends of an entry, which turns ' bay' into 'bay'. Lowercasing turns every capital into its small form, which turns 'BAY' into 'bay'. Once both have been done, the three spellings of Bay are one piece of text and Hill is unchanged.

A real sheet has thousands of entries, and writing a loop to tidy each one would be slow to write and slow to read. pandas has a shortcut for applying a text job to a whole column, which is where we go next.

steps.headline: One call for the whole column

lead.text: Put .str in front of a method and pandas applies that method to every entry in the Series. s.str.strip() strips each entry and s.str.lower() lowercases each one. The .str part is called an accessor. It is a doorway on the Series that opens onto the text methods, so you can skip the loop and ask for the job once.

The figure runs this on three entries that need tidying: ' Bay ', 'HILL' and ' lake'. The first case only strips them. The second chains another call on the end, so each entry is stripped and then lowercased.

afterFigure.text: Chaining works because every .str call returns a new Series, ready for the next call. It also means the original is untouched, so store the result if you want to keep it, for example clean = s.str.strip().str.lower(). Apply that to the tally sheet and the three spellings of Bay become one entry, which leaves two different shops in the column.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([' Bay ', 'HILL', ' lake'])
result = s.str.strip()

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([' Bay ', 'HILL', ' lake'])
result = s.str.strip().str.lower()

lead.text: strip removes blank characters at the ends, and lower changes capitals to small letters. Neither adds or removes a letter.

reveal.text: You cleaned the text before counting. Case conversion changes letters but keeps their number, so only the spaces were lost.

lead.text: Cleaning makes entries consistent, but a cell can still hold two facts. Suppose the supplier's export writes each row as 'Bay|east', the shop and its region joined by a bar. To count shops by region you need those two parts in separate columns.

s.str.split('|', expand=True) cuts every entry at the bar and gives each piece its own column. Without expand=True you would get a list of pieces inside each cell, which is awkward to use. The figure splits two small Series and names the new columns afterwards.

afterFigure.text: Both cases pass n=1, which tells split to stop after the first bar. In the first case every entry has one bar, so n=1 changes nothing. In the second case 'Bay|east|harbour' has two bars. The shop is 'Bay' and the rest, 'east|harbour', stays together in the second column. That matters when a later piece may contain the separator itself and should not be torn apart.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series(['Bay|east', 'Hill|west'])
parts = s.str.split('|', n=1, expand=True)
parts.columns = ['shop', 'region']

values.name: parts
values.display:
shop region
0   Bay   east
1  Hill   west

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series(['Bay|east|harbour', 'Hill|west'])
parts = s.str.split('|', n=1, expand=True)
parts.columns = ['shop', 'description']

values.name: parts
values.display:
shop   description
0   Bay  east|harbour
1  Hill          west

steps.headline: Split ['Bay|east|harbour', 'Hill|west|dock'] once at '|' with expand=True. What does the second column hold?

workedSteps.text: n=1 splits at the first '|' only. The first column is the shop.
The second column keeps everything after that first '|'.

steps.headline: Splitting each of two strings once with expand=True gives a small table. How many cells does it hold?

workedSteps.text: Each string splits into two fields. How many columns does the result have?
There is one row per string. How many cells is that in total?

steps.headline: A rule of your own for every value

lead.text: The .str methods cover cleaning and splitting, but sometimes you need a rule they do not offer. Say each entry lists colours, as in 'red,blue', and you want the number of colours in each. Series.map takes a function and calls it once on every value, then collects the answers into a new Series. A lambda is a small function written on one line, and lambda text: len(text.split(',')) splits an entry at its commas and counts the pieces.
The figure has two versions of the same job.

afterFigure.text: The first case uses map, so the function is called once per entry. The second needs no function at all. s.str.count(',') + 1 counts the commas in each entry and adds one, because an entry with one comma holds two items. That is a vectorised operation: a single instruction that works on the whole column at once. Prefer it when it can express your rule, since it is shorter, easier to read and much faster on a long column. Keep map for rules that no built-in operation covers.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series(['red,blue', 'green'])
counts = s.map(lambda text: len(text.split(',')))

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series(['red,blue', 'green'])
counts = s.str.count(',') + 1

lead.text: Series.map is a method of one Series, and it calls the function once for each value in that Series. Decide what the function receives each time.
s.str.count(',') counts the commas in each value. One more than that is the number of items in a comma-separated list.

reveal.text: Counting separators gave the items per value in one vectorised step. You then added the counts to get the total.

steps.headline: Rules that need a whole row

lead.text: Some rules need more than one value at a time. To add the a column to the b column for each order, the function has to see both numbers from the same row. df.apply(f, axis=1) calls f once for each row, and inside f the expression row['a'] reads that row's value in column a. The axis=1 asks for one row at a time. The default, axis=0, would hand over whole columns instead.
The figure adds two columns both ways.

afterFigure.text: The first case uses apply with a lambda. The second does the same sum as df['a'] + df['b'] and then renames the new column with df.rename. Both give the same numbers. Use apply when the rule needs steps that column arithmetic cannot express, such as choosing between two formulas by the values in the row. When plain arithmetic on the columns will do, that is the form to write. The tally sheet is now tidy and split where it needed splitting, and any rule you add can be run row by row or on the whole column.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'a': [2, 4], 'b': [3, 6]})
df['total'] = df.apply(lambda row: row['a'] + row['b'], axis=1)

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'a': [2, 4], 'b': [3, 6]})
df['total'] = df['a'] + df['b']
df = df.rename(columns={'total': 'combined'})

lead.text: With axis=1, apply hands the function one row at a time. Inside it, row['a'] is that row's value in column a. Adding up the results is a separate step.

reveal.text: The function ran once for each row and combined that row's two values. The vectorised version does the same arithmetic without calling a function.

lesson.orientation: Clean and split strings, rename columns and choose vectorised or rowwise work.
lesson.reviewLabel: Turn messy text into usable columns
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: Picture a tally sheet from a market stall, filled in by three people over a week. One writes Bay. Another writes ' bay' with a space slipped in front, and a third writes 'BAY ' in capitals with a space at the end. Hill is written down once, tidily. A person reads that as two shops. A computer that compares text exactly sees four different pieces of text.

The last lesson was about gaps, which a table admits to by showing them as NaN. These slips are harder because they look like ordinary data, so nothing warns you and a count or a match goes quietly wrong. Some cells hold two facts squeezed into one, such as a shop and its region joined by a bar.
This lesson cleans the sheet until each shop is written one way. It then splits the cells that hold two facts, and ends with how to apply a rule of your own to every row.

intro.promise: By the end you'll clean and split text in a column, and know when a one-line operation replaces a loop.

recap.keyIdea: The .str accessor cleans and splits text for every row at once, and a vectorised operation does what a rowwise function would, in one step.

blocks.text: You cleaned the tally sheet until Bay appeared once, which left 2 different shops. Splitting two strings once made 4 cells, and a rowwise product over the rows (2, 3) and (4, 1) summed to 10.

recap.nextHook: Clean text is still only text. A date such as 03/04/2026 is text too, and it can be read two ways depending on who wrote it. The next lesson turns date strings into real dates by stating their format, and counts the entries that cannot be read at all.

questions.prompt: How many characters remain in '  NORTH '.strip().lower()?
hints: Trim the outside whitespace before counting.
Case conversion changes letters, not how many there are.
Count the letters of the cleaned word.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The cleaned string is north, which has five characters.

questions.onCorrect: 5. strip removed the spaces, and lower kept every letter, leaving five characters.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the spaces too. strip removes them.

questions.prompt: How many cells are in the result?
hints: Keep the row count separate from the field count.
Every string gives one row.
Multiply the rows by the columns.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two rows times two columns gives four cells.

questions.onCorrect: 4. Two rows of two fields fill four cells.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of rows or columns alone. Multiply the two.

questions.prompt: What does Series.map(lambda x: len(x)) pass to the function?
hints: Which object owns the method?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Series.map applies the function to each value in that Series.

questions.onCorrect: Each value of the Series. map calls the function once for every value.

misconceptions.feedback: map belongs to the Series, so it sees that Series' values, not the table.
map visits every value, not just the first.

questions.prompt: Rows have (a, b) of (2, 3) and (4, 1). What is df.apply(lambda row: row['a'] * row['b'], axis=1).sum()?
hints: With axis=1 the function sees one row at a time.
Multiply a by b within each row.
Add the two row results.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The row products are 6 and 4, and they sum to 10.

questions.onCorrect: 10. The function gave 6 for the first row and 4 for the second, and the sum added them.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the column sums. The function works one row at a time.
That is only the first row. Both rows are processed.

hints: Count the parts, not the delimiters.
Each separator divides two neighbouring parts.
Write the strings between the commas and count them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Splitting at the two commas produces three items.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Two commas split the text into three parts.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the commas. There is one more part than there are separators.

questions.prompt: A row has a = 7 and b = 9. What is row['a'] + row['b']?
hints: Use the two values from the same row.
With axis=1, both operands come from one row.
Add the row's a value to its b value.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The row calculation adds 7 and 9 to give 16.

questions.onCorrect: 16. The function sees one whole row, so both of its values are available together.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies. The function adds the two values.

hints: Strip each value first.
Count the letters in each cleaned value.
Add the two lengths.
questions.prompt: s holds ' Ab ' and 'cD'. What is s.str.strip().str.len().sum()?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The cleaned values are 'Ab' and 'cD', with 2 + 2 = 4 characters.

questions.onCorrect: 4. Stripping leaves two letters in each value, so the lengths add up to 4.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the spaces in the first value. strip removes them.

hints: Which three entries are really the same shop?
Spaces and capitals do not make a new shop.
Count Bay once and Hill once.
questions.prompt: How many different shops does the sheet list once the slips are ignored?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The three Bay spellings are one shop, and Hill is the other.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Spaces and capitals are slips, not differences, so Bay appears once. In pandas you clean them with strip and lower.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every spelling as a new shop. The slips of the pen are not real differences.
All three Bay spellings are the same shop.

hints: String operations hand back new values.
questions.prompt: What does s.str.strip() do to s itself?

choices.label: Nothing: it returns a new Series

acceptedIdeas: Nothing: it returns a new Series
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: str.strip returns new values and leaves s unchanged.

questions.onCorrect: Nothing. It returns a new Series, so assign the result if you want to keep it.

misconceptions.feedback: String operations do not edit in place. They return new values.
Nothing is deleted. s still exists unchanged.

hints: What would a second split do to 'east|harbour'?
questions.prompt: Why split only once with n=1?

choices.label: Later text may contain the separator too, and should stay together

acceptedIdeas: Later text may contain the separator too, and should stay together
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: n=1 splits at the first separator only.

questions.onCorrect: Later text may contain the separator too. Limiting the splits keeps it together.

misconceptions.feedback: A string can be split many times. n=1 limits it on purpose.
No characters are removed except the separator.

hints: Each string is split once.
One split makes two pieces.
Each piece becomes a column.
questions.prompt: How many columns does the result have?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One split gives two fields, so two columns.

questions.onCorrect: 2. One split makes two pieces, and expand=True gives each piece its own column.

misconceptions.feedback: expand=True turns the pieces into separate columns, so there is more than one.

hints: Count the commas in each value, then add one.
The values hold two, one and three items.
Add the three item counts.
questions.prompt: For the values 'a,b', 'c' and 'd,e,f', what is the total of the item counts?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The item counts are 2, 1 and 3, totalling 6.

questions.onCorrect: 6. The values hold 2, 1 and 3 items, and counting commas plus one gives each in one step.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of values, and also the number of commas. Add up the items in each value.
